red_flags.text: Hypotension or tachycardia after a high-energy mechanism with pelvic or groin pain.
Blood at the urethral meatus, perineal or scrotal haematoma, or a high-riding prostate: suspect urethral injury and do not pass a catheter blindly.
A wound in the perineum, groin, buttock, vagina or rectum: an open pelvic fracture, with very high mortality.
Leg-length discrepancy or rotation without a hip or femoral fracture.
An older anticoagulated patient after a low-energy fall can still bleed from the pelvis.
A negative CT with a binder on: a well-applied binder can hide a catastrophic ring injury.

do_now.text: If active bleeding from a pelvic fracture is suspected after blunt high-energy trauma, apply a purpose-made pelvic binder.
Centre the binder over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests.
Give intravenous tranexamic acid as soon as possible, ideally within an hour of injury; do not start it more than 3 hours after injury unless there is evidence of hyperfibrinolysis.
Resuscitate the unstable patient with blood products through the massive transfusion protocol.
If received in a trauma unit, resuscitate and transfer immediately to a major trauma centre for definitive control of bleeding.

assess.text: Primary survey with the binder on. Do not spring or rock the pelvis: it adds nothing and dislodges clot.
Inspect perineum, and examine rectum and vagina when an open fracture is suspected.
Lower limb neurology, for lumbosacral plexus injury.
Shock index trend is more useful than a single blood pressure.

investigate.text: High-energy trauma: contrast CT of head, chest, abdomen and pelvis with a head-to-toe scanogram. A contrast blush means active arterial bleeding.
In the non-responder, limit imaging to the minimum needed to direct intervention. A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
Post-binder pelvic radiograph after resuscitation in every polytrauma patient, even with a 'negative' CT.
Suspected urethral injury: retrograde urethrography per the urological trauma BOAST.

resuscitate.text: Minimise heat loss: warm the patient, the fluids and the room.
Keep the binder on during any surgery; do not remove it for a post-binder radiograph until the patient is haemodynamically stable.
Rapidly reverse anticoagulation in a bleeding patient.

definitive.text: Active arterial pelvic haemorrhage: interventional radiology with selective embolisation, unless immediate open surgery is needed for bleeding elsewhere.
Non-responder to resuscitation: surgical (preperitoneal) packing or angioembolisation, according to the major trauma centre protocol.
Preperitoneal packing is usually combined with mechanical stabilisation, such as an anterior external fixator, so the packs have something to press against.
Arterial contrast extravasation on CT may need angiography and embolisation even when the patient is currently stable.
Use external fixation for temporary stabilisation when early definitive surgery is not possible, and consider traction for a displaced vertical shear injury.
Remove the binder ideally within 24 hours of injury, under a network protocol; reconstruct the ring within 72 hours of physiological stabilisation if associated injuries allow.
Open fractures with perineal or rectal wounds: urgent general or colorectal consultant review, debridement per the open fracture standard, and consider a defunctioning stoma.

escalate.text: Haemodynamic instability with a pelvic fracture is a major trauma centre problem. Transfer early rather than after the CT.
Call interventional radiology at the same time as the trauma team, not after the scan is reported.
Urology for any suspected bladder or urethral injury before instrumentation.

notes: Most pelvic bleeding is venous and from fracture surfaces, which is why mechanical stability and packing work and why embolisation alone does not stop every bleed.
The binder is a resuscitation device. It belongs on in the ambulance, stays on through theatre, and comes off under a plan.
REBOA is used in some centres as a bridge to definitive haemorrhage control; it is a team capability, not an individual one.
